name: Dana Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a shift lead at Hartfield Biscuits, out on the industrial estate past the ring road. I run two lines, from the dough mixer through a sixty-metre tunnel oven to the wrapping machines, and I've got nine people on my shift. Most of my day is adjusting things: oven zones, belt speed, the wrapper's film tension, because a biscuit that's a millimetre too thick jams the whole packer. I love the smell for about ten minutes, then you stop noticing it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part and the worst part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best part is a clean shift where we hit the count and nobody gets hurt. Worst part is allergen changeovers, when we switch from a plain line to one with nuts and everything has to be stripped and swabbed, and the clock is screaming at you. I live with my partner Theo, he drives buses, and we've got about four months' money put by. I'm in the union, I go to meetings, but I'm not the loud one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, so mostly nothing. I can picture that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a relief, now can we talk about the real problems, like the heat in the packing hall and the shift pattern. I'd probably say it in the group chat with a sarcastic face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I already use AI a bit. I ask it to tidy up my handover notes and sometimes to explain a fault code in the wrapper's manual. If it stays at that level, it's a handy helper and that's it. Our real automation worry is the robot packers the company looked at last year, and that's got nothing to do with hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal, keep my savings ticking up by about a hundred and fifty a month, and keep going to union meetings. Theo and I would stick with the plan to look at buying a small place in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little bit flat, maybe, like waiting for a big storm that just drizzles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the robot packers.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A sales rep came in with a video of arms picking biscuits off the belt and dropping them in trays, ten times faster than Rosa and the girls. Management priced it, and it came back too expensive for us, for now. Rosa's fifty-four. She asked me afterwards if she should start looking, and I didn't know what to tell her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you tell her in the end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I said, not yet, but keep your ears open, and I'd tell her the minute I heard anything. That's the thing about being a lead. You're not management but people look at you like you know something.

S0.say: She'd say it's a relief and turn the talk to real problems like heat in the packing hall and shift patterns. She'd likely joke about it in the work group chat.
S0.think: She already uses AI now and then for handover notes and fault codes and sees it as a small helper if it stays like this. Her real worry is the robot packers the company already priced, which don't depend on the hype.
S0.do: Carries on as normal and keeps adding about one hundred and fifty a month to savings. Keeps going to union meetings and sticks with the plan to buy a small place in two years.
S0.feel: Calm, a little flat, like a storm that only drizzles.
S0.quote: You're not management but people look at you like you know something.
S0.fieldNote: Dana already uses AI casually and doesn't fear it as software. Her concern is physical automation of the packing team, and especially an older colleague who asked her for advice. She carries the weight of being in the middle between management and the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah. This one feels like it's already started at our place, a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is fine if it's done with us and not to us. I'd want the union in the room before any new kit is bought, and I'd say that at the next meeting, maybe louder than I usually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, I think I'd be okay. Leads who can handle the computers usually get kept to run the new lines. It's Rosa and the packers I'd worry about. They're the ones a robot replaces first, and some of them have been there twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get better at the AI tools on purpose, not just for notes, so I could be the person who sets up and checks new systems on the line. I'd ask the union rep to put new technology on the agenda in the next three months. And I'd keep saving, maybe up to two hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like the low whine the oven fans make before one goes. You hear it but you keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Rosa in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her straight that the packing side is going to shrink, and help her get on the list for the quality checker job, because that needs people who know what a bad biscuit looks like. She does. She can spot a cracked one at belt speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change anything at home, with Theo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much. Theo's bus might get some new route software, he'd moan about it. We'd still look for a place, maybe just a cheaper one, further out.

S1.say: She'd say change is fine if it's done with workers rather than to them. She'd push for the union to be involved before any new equipment is bought.
S1.think: She believes leads who can handle computers will be kept to run new lines, so she feels fairly safe. Her worry is for the packers, some with twenty years in, who would be replaced first.
S1.do: Learns AI tools properly so she can set up and check new systems on the line. Asks the union rep to put new technology on the agenda within three months and raises savings to two hundred a month.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a background whine from an oven fan that might be failing.
S1.quote: She can spot a cracked one at belt speed.
S1.fieldNote: Dana's first thought is for others on her shift, not herself. She plans to adapt in a measured way by getting good at the tools she already dabbles in. The union is her route for protecting the packers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's shocking. That's before we'd even have bought a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments to step in, now. Pay people while they find their feet, tax the companies doing the replacing. I'd share union posts about it and turn up to whatever the union organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared. If a robot can do a changeover and swab a line and read a fault code, then the whole shift is gone, me included. Four months of savings sounds okay until you realise there'd be thousands of us looking at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the flat savings and turn them into an emergency fund straight away, and cut the takeaways and the car loan plans. I'd get involved properly with the union, actually stand up and speak, push for redundancy terms and retraining money. If it came to it, Theo and I would move in with my mum for a year to keep our heads above water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car. We were going to get a second one so I don't have to wait for the night bus after late shift. That's gone. Then takeaways, then the gym. Theo would keep his football, that's his sanity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'if it came to it' about moving in with your mum. When would it come to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The day they gave us dates. Mum's got a spare room in the town I grew up in, forty minutes away. I wouldn't love it, Theo definitely wouldn't love it, but it's better than burning through four months and then having nothing.

S2.say: She'd call for urgent government action, including income support for workers and taxes on companies doing the replacing. She'd share union posts and turn up to union actions.
S2.think: She'd be scared that a capable robot would take the whole shift, including her. She sees that four months of savings won't stretch far if thousands lose work at once.
S2.do: Turns flat savings into an emergency fund and cuts takeaways and plans for a second car. Speaks up actively in the union for redundancy terms and retraining money, and would move in with her mother for a year if dates were announced.
S2.quote: Four months of savings sounds okay until you realise there'd be thousands of us looking at the same time.
S2.fieldNote: The fast version flips Dana from quietly confident to genuinely frightened. She moves quickly from union talk to very concrete household cuts. Family is her backstop, though she clearly dislikes having to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, I can breathe a bit more with that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, we need a plan from government, but I'd also say to people: use the time. Don't wait for the letter. I'd say that to my shift, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years is enough for me to learn something they'd still need people for, at least for a while. I've always fancied the maintenance side, the engineers who fix the lines. Those jobs would last longer than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for an evening course in industrial maintenance, the electrical side, at the college by the bus station, about two nights a week. I'd keep building savings to six months. I'd also push the union to get the company to pay for courses for everyone, not just leads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a busy kind of anxious. Like a changeover. You've got a list and a clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the maintenance side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when a line goes down, everyone stands around until Gav from maintenance turns up with his laptop and his spanner. Even with robots, someone has to fix the robots for a while. I'd rather be Gav than the person the robot replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And after 2031, when it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I don't know. Maybe the robots fix each other by then. I'd have bought myself a few years, and that's something. I'm not going to pretend I've got the end of the story.

S3.say: She'd repeat the call for a government plan but urge people, including her shift, to use the time rather than wait for bad news.
S3.think: She thinks five years is enough to move into maintenance work that would last longer than her current job, at least for a while. She has always been drawn to the engineers who fix the lines.
S3.do: Starts an evening industrial maintenance course two nights a week in the first year and builds savings to six months. Pushes the union to get the company to fund courses for all staff, not only leads.
S3.feel: Anxious but busy and organised, like working through a changeover with a list and a clock.
S3.quote: Even with robots, someone has to fix the robots for a while. I'd rather be Gav than the person the robot replaced.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Dana turns fear into a concrete plan: retraining as a maintenance technician. She is honest that this only buys time and that she doesn't know what happens after. She still pushes for collective support for the wider shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a real stretch of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly, so no excuses. Governments should be setting up retraining, shorter weeks, all of that. I'd vote for whoever had an actual plan, not whoever shouted loudest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years feels manageable. I could do the maintenance course and maybe even a further qualification. The thing that would change most is whether Theo and I have kids. That's the bit ten years really touches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the maintenance course within the year, without panicking about it, and maybe aim for the full engineering certificate after. We'd buy the flat, but a cheaper one so the mortgage stays low. I'd vote and campaign for a party with a serious plan for retraining and income support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly hopeful, but there's a question mark over the end of it I can't get rid of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said kids. What would you be weighing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether I want a seven-year-old when nobody has jobs. That sounds dramatic. But in this version, when they're grown, what do they do? Theo says people always find something. I want to believe him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is ten years better or worse for you than five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. Five is a sprint, ten is a plan. With ten, I'm not just saving myself, I can actually think about the next part of life instead of grabbing whatever's nearest.

S4.say: She'd say ten years leaves no excuse for not handling it fairly, with retraining and shorter working weeks. She'd vote for whoever had a real plan rather than whoever shouted loudest.
S4.think: She finds ten years manageable for retraining and possibly a further qualification. The biggest effect is on whether she and her partner have children.
S4.do: Starts the maintenance course within the year and considers a full engineering certificate after. Buys a cheaper flat to keep the mortgage low, and votes and campaigns for a party with a serious retraining plan.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly hopeful, with a question mark over the end she can't shake.
S4.quote: Five is a sprint, ten is a plan.
S4.fieldNote: For Dana, the long timeline moves the question from her job to her family plans. She is steady rather than eager, and the decade lets her retrain without panic. Her doubt about having children is quiet but real.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because it's the worst ending, they all end the same, but because there's no time to do anything except panic. What would help is money while you retrain, and the company being made to pay for the training, not just the government.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the older ones. Everyone asks people like me, the ones with a diploma and time. Rosa's fifty-four with no diploma at all. Whatever happens, she's the one I'd be thinking about on the drive home.

headlineQuote: Rosa's fifty-four with no diploma at all. Whatever happens, she's the one I'd be thinking about on the drive home.
portrait: Dana Jensen is twenty-seven, a shift lead on two biscuit lines at a food factory, living with her partner Theo, a bus driver, with about four months' savings. She uses AI tools now and then and is open to change once it's proven, which shows in her measured plans. She is calm when AI stalls and uneasy with steady change, and her first thoughts are for the older packers on her shift. AGI in two years leaves her alarmed and planning cuts and a move back to her mother's, while five and ten years push her into a maintenance course. The ten-year picture worries her less for her job than for whether to have children.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there would be no time to do anything except panic.
whatWouldHelp: Money to live on while retraining, with companies, not only the government, made to pay for the training.
